intro: Long before 1492, the Americas were home to great cities and empires. The Aztec built an island capital with floating gardens. The Maya carved the histories of their kings in stone and invented the zero. The Inca ran an empire along the Andes with roads, runners and knotted cords. Each society ranked people, from rulers and nobles down to commoners, and each asked the many to work for the few.

After 1492, Spain and Portugal built colonies that sorted people by birthplace and ancestry. Millions of Indigenous people died of disease and forced labor. About 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships and carried into slavery. People inside these systems pushed back in many ways, from daily acts to the Haitian Revolution, until slavery was abolished across the Americas by 1888.

In this unit you will compare how these societies organized power and work. You will read primary sources and data with a careful eye. You will describe achievements and hard truths fairly. By the end, you will be able to explain how ranks were built, how people resisted them, and why their effects can still be seen.
bigQuestion: How did societies in the Americas rank people, and how did people resist and change those ranks?

title: Societies of the Americas

chapters.title: The Aztec, the Maya and the Inca
chapters.bigQuestion: How did the great societies of the early Americas organize people, work and power?

story.title: A Morning in the Great Market
story.kicker: A trader steps into the market of Tlatelolco, beside Tenochtitlan, and hears thousands of voices at once.
paragraphs: The canoe slides up to the stone edge of the island city. The trader climbs out with a bundle of cotton cloth on his back. The sun is still low over Lake Texcoco, but the causeways are already busy. People walk in from the shore along the raised roads. Canoes loaded with maize, flowers and firewood crowd the canals. Ahead of him rise white temples, and beyond them the snowy volcanoes stand against the sky.

He turns toward the market of Tlatelolco, the sister city joined to Tenochtitlan. Before he can see it, he can hear it. Thousands of voices bargain, call out prices and greet old friends. The noise rolls over the plaza like surf. Each kind of goods has its own row. Here are sellers of turkeys and rabbits. There are sellers of chili peppers, beans and tomatoes. Farther on are pottery, sandals, feathers, obsidian blades and jade beads.

Money here is not coins. People trade goods for goods. Small things are often priced in cacao beans, the seeds used to make chocolate. Larger things may be priced in lengths of cotton cloth. The trader knows this well. He watches a woman count out cacao beans for a pile of chili peppers. Market judges walk the rows. If a seller cheats with a false measure, the judges can punish him on the spot.

The trader finds his place and lays out his cloth. He belongs to a guild of long-distance merchants. His group has walked for weeks to distant towns and come home with news as well as goods. Around him are farmers, craftworkers, nobles and servants, all in one crowd. In a single market, he can see the whole order of his society. Each person has a place in it, and each place comes with its own work and its own rules.
story.think: The trader could see his whole society in one market. What could a visitor learn about your community by watching one busy place for a morning?

lessons.title: A City on a Lake
lessons.mainIdea: The Mexica built Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco and fed it with farm plots built on the water.
reading: The people we often call the Aztec called themselves the *Mexica*. Around 1325 they founded their city, Tenochtitlan, on a small island in Lake Texcoco, in the Valley of Mexico. The land was swampy and hard to use. In less than two hundred years, the Mexica turned it into one of the largest cities in the world. Mexico City stands on the same spot today.

To grow food, farmers built *chinampas*. A chinampa was a long, narrow garden made by piling mud and plants inside a fence of stakes in shallow water. Trees planted at the edges held the soil in place. Canals ran between the plots, so farmers could move crops by canoe. Chinampas could give several harvests a year of maize, beans, squash and flowers.

Three long *causeways*, or raised roads, linked the island to the shore. An aqueduct carried fresh water from springs at Chapultepec. By about 1500, Tenochtitlan may have held around 200,000 people, though historians give different estimates. In 1428 it joined two other cities in the Triple Alliance. Together they built an empire that collected tribute from many peoples across central Mexico.

words.d: the people, often called the Aztec, who founded Tenochtitlan and led the Aztec Empire
long garden plots built up from mud and plants in shallow lake water
raised roads built across water or wet ground

look.title: A Garden in the Water

look.prompt: Why would building farms on the lake help a city on an island grow large?

choices: On an island in Lake Texcoco

check.why: Causeways were raised roads that connected the island to the land around the lake. The aqueduct carried the water.

lessons.title: Nobles and Commoners
lessons.mainIdea: Aztec society was divided mainly into nobles, called pipiltin, and commoners, called macehualtin, each with different duties.
reading: At the top of Mexica society was the *huey tlatoani*, or great speaker, the ruler of Tenochtitlan. Below him were the *pipiltin*, the nobles. Nobles served as officials, judges, priests and army leaders. They could own land worked by others. They wore finer cotton clothes and could live in stone houses. Noble boys often went to a school called the calmecac, where they studied religion, history and law.

Most people were *macehualtin*, or commoners. They farmed, fished, built, made crafts and served as soldiers. Commoners belonged to a local group called a calpolli, a neighborhood of related families. The calpolli gave each family land to farm and ran a school for its boys. In return, commoners paid tribute in goods and gave labor for public works like temples and dikes.

The line between the groups was strong, but not closed. A commoner who captured enemies in war could win honors, better clothing and gifts of land. Laws also set out duties for nobles, and they could be punished harshly for crimes. Supporters of this order saw it as a fair trade of service for protection. Critics, then and now, point out that commoners carried most of the heavy work.

words.d: the great speaker, the title of the ruler of Tenochtitlan
the Aztec nobles, who served as officials, judges, priests and commanders
the Aztec commoners, who farmed, worked and paid tribute

look.title: Two Families, One City
look.text: Family A lives in a stone house near the great temple. The father judges cases in a court. His son studies history at the calmecac. Family B lives in a reed and mud house by the canals. They farm a chinampa given by their calpolli. Each year they send cloth and maize as tribute, and the father helps repair a dike.
look.prompt: Which family is pipiltin and which is macehualtin? Name two clues for each.

check.q: Who were the macehualtin?
choices: The nobles who served as judges and priests
The priests who ran the calmecac school
The commoners who farmed, worked and paid tribute
check.why: The reading says macehualtin were commoners who farmed, built, made crafts and paid tribute.

check.q: What was a calpolli?
choices: A local group of related families that shared land
A school only for noble boys
A market judge who checked measures
A raised road across the lake
check.why: A calpolli was a neighborhood group of related families. It gave families land and ran a school.

check.q: How could a commoner rise in Aztec society?
choices: By buying a noble title with cacao
check.why: The reading says a commoner who captured enemies could win honors, better clothing and land.

lessons.title: Merchants and Enslaved People
lessons.mainIdea: Pochteca merchants held a special place in Aztec society, and enslaved people had some rights their children could build on.
reading: The *pochteca* were long-distance merchants. They traveled in groups for weeks, carrying goods to far towns and bringing back feathers, jade, cacao and cotton. They were organized in guilds, with their own leaders and their own god. They also brought back news. Rulers sometimes used them as spies. Some pochteca grew very rich, but they were careful not to show off, because nobles did not want rivals.

The market rules were strict. Market judges, like the ones in the opening story, settled arguments and punished cheating. Most trade was barter, which means swapping goods for goods. Cacao beans and cotton cloth worked a bit like money for setting prices. The Aztec *tribute* system also moved goods: conquered towns sent cloth, food, feathers and other items to Tenochtitlan on a fixed schedule.

At the bottom of society were enslaved people, called tlacotin. A person could become enslaved for debt, as punishment for a crime, or by selling himself in hard times. Aztec slavery was harsh, but it differed from later slavery in the Americas. Enslaved people could marry and own some property. Their children were born free. Some were able to buy back their freedom.

words.d: Aztec long-distance merchants organized in guilds
goods or labor that a conquered or ruled people must pay to a ruler
trading goods for other goods without using money

look.title: A Spanish Visitor Sees the Market
look.text: Hernan Cortes wrote to the king of Spain that the great market square was twice the size of the main square of Salamanca. He said that more than sixty thousand people came each day to buy and sell, and that every kind of goods had its own street.
look.cite: Hernan Cortes, Second Letter to Emperor Charles V, 1520 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Cortes wanted the king's support. How might that goal shape how he described the city? What details still seem useful?

check.q: Who were the pochteca?
check.why: The pochteca were merchants who traveled far in groups and were organized in guilds.

check.q: Which statement about enslaved people in Aztec society matches the reading?
choices: Their status passed to all their descendants
They were all captured in foreign lands
check.why: The reading says children of enslaved people, or tlacotin, were born free, and some could buy their freedom.

check.q: In the Aztec market, what often served like money for small purchases?
check.why: Most trade was barter, but cacao beans and cotton cloth were used to set prices.

lessons.title: Kings and City-States
lessons.mainIdea: The Maya were never one empire; they lived in many city-states, each led by a holy king.
reading: Walk through the rainforest of northern Guatemala and you come to Tikal. Its stone temples rise above the treetops, some more than 60 meters high. During the Classic period, about 250 to 900 CE, Tikal was one of dozens of Maya cities spread across what is now southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and Honduras. Other great cities included Calakmul, Copan and Palenque.

The Maya did not form one empire. They lived in *city-states*, cities that each ruled the farms and villages around them. Each had its own ruler, called a k'uhul ajaw, or holy lord. People believed the king stood between them and the gods. Kings led ceremonies, went to war and built temples. Powerful cities like Tikal and Calakmul formed alliances and fought long wars against each other.

Kings left records on tall carved stones called *stelae*. One famous ruler, K'inich Janaab Pakal of Palenque, ruled for about 68 years in the 600s CE. His tomb, found in 1952 inside the Temple of the Inscriptions, held a jade mask. Below the kings were nobles, scribes, craftworkers and many farmers. Farmers grew maize, beans and squash and gave labor to build the great plazas.

words.d: independent cities that each rule the land and villages around them
tall carved stone slabs that record rulers and events
holy lord, the title of a Maya king

look.title: Rival Cities
look.text: Imagine two Maya cities a few days' walk apart. Each has its own king, its own temples and its own farms. One king carves a stela saying he defeated the other city. Years later, the other city carves its own stela about a victory of its own.
look.prompt: What does this tell you about how the Maya world was organized? Why should a historian read both stelae?

check.q: How was Maya political life organized in the Classic period?

In many city-states, each with its own king
In a republic with elected leaders
In villages with no rulers at all
check.why: The reading says the Maya never formed one empire. They lived in city-states, each led by a holy lord.

check.q: What are stelae?
choices: Farm plots built in lake water
Tall carved stones that record rulers and events
check.why: Maya kings left records on tall carved stones called stelae.

check.q: Which city was a powerful rival of Tikal?
check.why: The reading names Calakmul as a powerful city that fought long wars with Tikal. Cusco and Tenochtitlan were Inca and Aztec.

lessons.title: Writing, Numbers and Time
lessons.mainIdea: The Maya created a full writing system, a number system with zero and careful calendars.
reading: The Maya created one of the few full writing systems invented in the Americas. Scribes used *glyphs*, signs that could stand for whole words or for sounds. They carved glyphs on stone and painted them in books made of bark paper. Spanish priests burned many of these books in the 1500s. Only four are known to survive today. Scholars have learned to read most Maya glyphs since the 1970s and 1980s.

Maya counting used a base of 20, not 10. A dot stood for one, a bar stood for five, and a shell sign stood for *zero*. Zero let the Maya write large numbers by place value. Each step up in place was worth 20 times more. Very few ancient peoples anywhere had a symbol for zero, and the Maya developed theirs on their own.

Maya astronomers watched the sun, moon and Venus closely. They kept a 260-day ritual count and a 365-day solar year. The two ran side by side and lined up again every 52 years. They also kept the Long Count, which tracked days from a starting date far in the past. Many Maya cities in the southern lowlands were left empty between about 800 and 900 CE. But the Maya people did not vanish. Millions of Maya people live in Mexico and Central America today and speak Mayan languages.

words.d: written signs that stand for words or sounds
a number that means none; it also holds an empty place in a number
a way of writing numbers where a digit's position sets its worth

look.title: How Two Calendars Fit Together
rows: Years until both line up again
look.cite: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian, Living Maya Time (online exhibit)
look.prompt: If a child was born on a certain day in both calendars, how old would she be when that same pair of days came around again?

check.q: What base did Maya counting use?
check.why: The reading says Maya counting used a base of 20, with each place worth 20 times more.

check.q: Why was a symbol for zero so useful?
choices: It showed the name of each king
It let the Maya write large numbers by place value
It marked the edges of chinampas
It stood for the number five
check.why: Zero holds an empty place, so the Maya could write large numbers using place value. A bar stood for five.

check.q: What happened to the Maya people after many southern cities were left empty?
choices: All Maya people moved to Tenochtitlan
Maya people kept living in the region, and millions live there today
The Maya stopped speaking their languages by 900 CE
check.why: The reading says the Maya did not vanish. Millions live in Mexico and Central America today and speak Mayan languages.

lessons.title: The Sapa Inca and Cusco
lessons.mainIdea: The Inca built the largest empire in the Americas, ruled from Cusco by the Sapa Inca.
reading: High in the Andes Mountains of Peru sits the city of Cusco. In the early 1400s it was the center of a small kingdom. Then, from about 1438, a ruler named Pachacuti began a burst of conquest. His son and grandson went further. By the early 1500s the Inca ruled land stretching about 4,000 kilometers along western South America, from today's Ecuador to Chile. It was the largest empire in the Americas at the time.

The Inca called their empire *Tawantinsuyu*, meaning the four parts together. Its ruler was the *Sapa Inca*, the only Inca. People taught that he descended from Inti, the sun god. He owned, in principle, all land and herds. Below him came Inca nobles from Cusco, then local lords of conquered peoples, and then the great mass of farming and herding families.

The Inca ruled many peoples who spoke different languages. They made Quechua a shared language of government. Sometimes they moved whole communities to new places to settle or to break up resistance. They built stone temples, forts and estates with walls so finely fitted that no mortar was needed. Machu Picchu, built around 1450, may have been a royal estate for Pachacuti.

words.d: the Inca name for their empire, meaning the four parts together
the title of the Inca emperor, meaning the only Inca
a large state in which one ruler or people governs many other peoples

look.title: Stone Without Mortar
look.text: Picture a wall in Cusco. Huge gray stones, some with twelve sides, fit together so tightly that you cannot slide a knife blade between them. There is no cement. Earthquakes have shaken this city many times, yet many Inca walls still stand while later buildings above them have cracked.
look.prompt: What does a wall like this tell you about the skills and the organized labor of the Inca?

check.q: What was the Sapa Inca?
choices: The Inca name for their roads
A kin group of related families
The title of the Inca emperor
check.why: Sapa Inca means the only Inca, the title of the emperor who ruled from Cusco.

check.q: What does Tawantinsuyu mean?
check.why: The Inca called their empire Tawantinsuyu, the four parts together. Holy lord and great speaker are Maya and Aztec titles.

check.q: Which ruler began the rapid growth of the Inca Empire around 1438?
check.why: The reading says Pachacuti began a burst of conquest from about 1438. Pakal was a Maya king of Palenque.

lessons.title: Ayllu and Mit'a
lessons.mainIdea: Inca life rested on the ayllu, a kin group, and on mit'a, turns of labor owed to the state.
reading: A family in an Andean village belonged to an *ayllu*. An ayllu was a group of related families who shared land, herds and work. Members helped each other plant, harvest and build houses. The ayllu divided its fields among families each year by need. A bigger family got more land. This habit of sharing work, called reciprocity, was old in the Andes long before the Inca.

The Inca did not ask most people to pay taxes in money or goods. Instead they asked for labor. This labor tax was called *mit'a*, meaning a turn. Each household took turns working for the state for a set time. People farmed state and temple fields, built roads and bridges, served as soldiers, or worked in mines. While they worked, the state fed them, often with food and maize beer.

The harvest from state lands went into thousands of *storehouses*, called qollqa, built along roads and on hillsides. The stored food, cloth and tools fed armies and workers and helped in times of drought. Supporters describe this as a system that protected people from hunger. Critics point out that people had little choice about their work and that the state could move them far from home.

words.d: an Andean group of related families who shared land and work
the Inca labor tax, in which households took turns working for the state
buildings for keeping food and goods; the Inca called them qollqa
the habit of giving help and getting help back in return

look.title: A Turn of Work
look.text: It is a young man's turn for mit'a. He leaves his ayllu's fields and walks three days to help build a stone bridge. Officials give him food and drink each day. When his turn ends, he walks home. His neighbors have kept his family's crops weeded while he was gone.
look.prompt: What did the young man give, and what did he get back from the state and from his ayllu?

check.q: What was mit'a?
choices: A tax paid in gold coins
A labor tax in which households took turns working for the state
check.why: Mit'a means a turn. Households took turns working on state fields, roads, armies or mines.

check.q: How did an ayllu divide its fields?
choices: By lottery once in a lifetime
By need, so bigger families got more land
check.why: The reading says the ayllu divided fields each year by need, so a bigger family got more land.

check.q: What is one criticism of the Inca labor system named in the reading?
choices: People had little choice about their work and could be moved far from home
It stored no food for hard times
It let merchants control the empire
It used cacao beans as money
check.why: Critics point out that people had little choice and the state could move them, even though storehouses helped in drought.

lessons.title: Roads, Runners and Quipu
lessons.mainIdea: A vast road system, relay runners and knotted cords called quipu held the Inca Empire together.
reading: The Inca built a road network called the *Qhapaq Nan*, or royal road. It ran along the coast and through the high mountains, with many branches. UNESCO describes it as more than 30,000 kilometers long. Workers cut stairs into cliffs and built rope bridges over deep canyons. Rest houses called tambos stood about a day's walk apart. The roads were for armies, officials and llama caravans, not for private travelers.

Messages moved by relay. Runners called *chasqui* waited at small posts along the roads. One runner sprinted to the next post and passed his message on. The next runner carried it on. In this way, news could cross the empire far faster than one person could walk. The Inca had no wheeled carts and no horses, so feet and llamas carried everything.

The Inca did not use written letters as the Maya did. Instead, record keepers used the *quipu*, a main cord with many hanging strings. Knots in the strings stood for numbers in a base-10 system. Colors and positions may have shown what was counted: people, llamas, or bags of maize. Experts called quipucamayoc read and made them. Scholars still debate whether quipu also recorded words and stories.

words.d: the Inca road network, meaning the royal road
Inca relay runners who carried messages along the roads
a set of knotted cords the Inca used to keep records

look.title: A Drawing of a Record Keeper
look.text: Around 1615, the Andean writer Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala drew an Inca official holding a large quipu. He explained that such officials kept accounts of the storehouses and of people across the kingdom with their knotted cords.
look.cite: Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, The First New Chronicle and Good Government, c. 1615 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Guaman Poma was Andean and wrote after the Spanish conquest. Why is his account useful, and what might it leave out?

check.q: What was a quipu?
choices: A carved stone that recorded a king
A set of knotted cords used to keep records
A garden plot in shallow water
check.why: A quipu was a main cord with hanging strings. Knots stood for numbers.

check.q: How did chasqui runners move messages so fast?
choices: By sending letters in wheeled carts
By relay, passing the message from runner to runner
check.why: Chasqui waited at posts and passed messages on in a relay. The Inca had no horses or wheeled carts.

check.q: What question about quipu do scholars still debate?
choices: Whether the Inca built any roads
Whether quipu used knots at all
Whether the Inca had any record keepers
Whether quipu also recorded words and stories
check.why: The reading says quipu recorded numbers, and scholars still debate whether they also recorded words.

lessons.title: Great Achievements
lessons.mainIdea: The Aztec, Maya and Inca each built lasting achievements in farming, science, building and government.
reading: Much of the food the world eats today was first grown by farmers of the Americas. Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, beans, squash, chili peppers and cacao all come from here. Andean farmers bred thousands of kinds of potatoes and built *terraces*, flat steps cut into steep hillsides. The terraces held soil and water in place. Aztec chinampas fed a city of many thousands.

Each society had its own strengths. The Maya built a full writing system, the number zero and precise calendars. The Aztec built a great island city with causeways and an aqueduct. The Inca built thousands of kilometers of road and ran a huge empire without written letters. They did all this without iron tools, draft animals like oxen, or wheeled vehicles for work.

Their stories were also written down. The *Popol Vuh* is a book of the K'iche' Maya of Guatemala. It tells how the gods made the world and people. It was written in the K'iche' language in Latin letters in the mid-1500s. Many Nahuatl speakers helped create the Florentine Codex around 1577, which records Aztec life in words and pictures. These works let us hear these peoples in their own voices.

words.d: flat steps of farmland cut into a hillside to hold soil and water
a sacred book of the K'iche' Maya that tells how the world and people were made

look.title: People Made of Maize
look.text: In the Popol Vuh, the makers first try to shape people from mud, and then from wood, but these people fail. At last they grind yellow and white maize and make the first true people from it.
look.cite: Popol Vuh, K'iche' Maya, written down c. 1550s (paraphrased summary)
look.prompt: Why might a farming people tell a story in which humans are made of maize?

check.q: What are terraces?
choices: Flat steps of farmland cut into a hillside
check.why: Terraces are flat steps cut into steep hillsides that hold soil and water.

check.q: What is the Popol Vuh?
choices: A sacred book of the K'iche' Maya
A Spanish letter to the king
check.why: The Popol Vuh is a K'iche' Maya book, written in the mid-1500s, that tells how the world and people were made.

check.q: Which achievement belongs to the Inca, according to the reading?
choices: Inventing a full glyph writing system
Building an island city with an aqueduct
Running a huge empire with thousands of kilometers of road
check.why: The reading credits the Inca with their road network and huge empire. Glyphs and the Popol Vuh are Maya; the island city is Aztec.

lessons.title: Hierarchies and Hard Truths
lessons.mainIdea: These societies had strict hierarchies, tribute and war, and a fair history names both the achievements and the costs.
reading: A *hierarchy* is a ranking of people from top to bottom. The Aztec, Maya and Inca all had one. Rulers and nobles held power and wealth. Commoners did most of the farming and building. In each place, people were taught that this order came from the gods. That belief helped keep it stable for many generations.

These empires also grew through war and tribute. The Aztec took captives in war, and many were killed in religious sacrifice at the great temple. Conquered towns resented heavy tribute. When Spanish soldiers arrived in 1519, thousands of Tlaxcalans and others who opposed the Aztec joined them. The Inca were fighting a civil war between two brothers when Francisco Pizarro captured the ruler Atahualpa in 1532.

Historians try to hold two truths at once. These were creative societies that built cities, sciences and systems that still amaze people today. They were also ruled by powerful few who asked much of the many, as were most societies of the time, including those of Europe. Judging fairly means using the same standard for every society and listening to evidence from all sides, including the voices of the peoples themselves.

words.d: a ranking of people or groups from highest to lowest
an offering to gods; among the Aztec, it included killing captives in ceremonies

look.title: Two Views of One City
look.text: Visitor A says: Tenochtitlan was a wonder, cleaner and larger than most cities in Europe, with gardens, canals and a huge market. Visitor B, from a town that pays tribute, says: Tenochtitlan takes our cloth and our young men, and we would be glad to see its power end.
look.prompt: Can both visitors be telling the truth? What would a fair historian do with both accounts?

check.q: What is a hierarchy?
choices: A trade of goods for goods
A calendar that repeats every 52 years
A ranking of people from highest to lowest
check.why: A hierarchy is a ranking of people or groups from top to bottom, as in all three societies.

check.q: Why did many Tlaxcalans join the Spanish in 1519?
choices: They opposed Aztec rule and its heavy tribute
They were paid in Inca gold
They wanted to protect Aztec temples
check.why: The reading says conquered and rival peoples resented Aztec tribute, and thousands of Tlaxcalans joined the Spanish.

check.q: What does the reading say a fair historian does?
choices: Uses the same standard for every society and listens to all sides
Judges only by what Spanish writers said
check.why: The reading says judging fairly means using one standard for every society and hearing evidence from all sides.

review.q: Which pair matches each group with its home region?
choices: Aztec: Andes Mountains; Inca: Valley of Mexico
Aztec: Valley of Mexico; Inca: Andes Mountains
review.why: The Aztec built Tenochtitlan in the Valley of Mexico. The Inca ruled from Cusco in the Andes.

review.q: What did the pipiltin and the macehualtin have in common?
choices: Both were kinds of farm plots
Both were ranks within Aztec society
review.why: Pipiltin were Aztec nobles and macehualtin were Aztec commoners, two ranks in one society.

review.q: How was the Maya political world different from the Inca one?
choices: The Maya had many city-states; the Inca had one empire
The Maya had one empire; the Inca had many city-states
Both had one ruler over everyone
review.why: Maya cities each had their own holy king, while the Inca ruled one large empire from Cusco.

review.q: Which record-keeping tool matches its society?
review.why: The Inca kept records on knotted quipu cords. The Maya wrote in glyphs and carved stelae.

review.q: How did the Inca mostly collect taxes?
choices: Through cacao beans sent to Cusco
Through mit'a, turns of labor for the state
Through a tax on horses and carts
review.why: The Inca labor tax, mit'a, asked households to take turns working for the state.

review.q: Which statement about Aztec slavery matches the chapter?
choices: Enslaved people could never be freed
Children of enslaved people were born free
review.why: The chapter says tlacotin could marry and own some property, their children were born free, and some bought freedom.

review.q: A student says the Maya disappeared around 900 CE. What is the best correction?
choices: Many southern cities were left empty, but millions of Maya people live today
The Maya moved to the Andes and joined the Inca
The Maya were conquered by the Aztec in 900 CE
The student is right; no Maya remain
review.why: Many southern lowland cities were abandoned, but Maya people kept living in the region and still speak Mayan languages.

review.q: Which sentence best shows a fair, balanced view of these societies?
choices: They had only achievements and no problems
They built great cities and sciences, and their rulers also asked much of commoners
They had only cruelty and no achievements
They were all the same society with different names
review.why: The chapter asks readers to hold two truths: real achievements and real hierarchies and costs.

chapters.title: Colonies, Castas and Slavery
chapters.bigQuestion: How did colonial rule sort people into ranks, and how did people resist and change those ranks?

story.title: Sixteen Panels
story.kicker: In Mexico City around 1760, a painter is paid to paint sixteen labels for sixteen kinds of people.
paragraphs: The workshop smells of linseed oil. A painter in Mexico City has sixteen canvases leaning against the wall. A wealthy customer has ordered a full set of casta paintings. Each canvas will show a family: a father, a mother and a child. Along the bottom of each, the painter will letter a label. The label names the parents' groups and gives a name to the child's group.

He starts with the first panel. A Spanish father and an Indigenous mother stand in a bright room with their small son. The label reads: from Spaniard and Indian, mestizo. On the next canvas, a Spanish father and an African mother hold a daughter. The label reads: from Spaniard and Black, mulato. Panel by panel, the labels grow longer and stranger, naming mixtures of mixtures.

The painter works carefully. He paints fine clothes on the families near the start of the set. Toward the end, the clothes grow plainer, the rooms poorer, and some families argue. The customer did not ask for real portraits of real neighbors. He asked for a picture of an idea: that people could be sorted by ancestry into ranks, with Spaniards at the top.

Outside the workshop, real life is messier. The painter's own street is full of people whose families mix every group on the canvases. Some rich merchants have mixed ancestry. Some Spaniards are poor. People often describe themselves differently to different officials. The paintings will be shipped to Spain, where collectors will look at them as a picture of New Spain. What they show is how the rulers wished society looked, not exactly how it was.
story.think: The painter was paid to paint an idea about people. Why might the people who held power want pictures like these to exist?

lessons.title: Spain and Portugal Divide the Americas
lessons.mainIdea: After 1492, Spain and Portugal claimed most of Central and South America and set up colonies ruled from Europe.
reading: In 1492 Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean. Two years later, in the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494, Spain and Portugal agreed on a line to divide the lands they expected to claim. Portugal received the eastern part, which became Brazil. Spain claimed most of the rest. The peoples who already lived there were not asked.

A *colony* is a land ruled by a distant country. Spain conquered the Aztec capital in 1521 and began the conquest of the Inca in 1532. It ruled its huge American lands through *viceroyalties*. Each was led by a viceroy, who governed in the king's name. The Viceroyalty of New Spain was ruled from Mexico City. The Viceroyalty of Peru was ruled from Lima.

Colonies were meant to make money for the ruling country. Silver was the great prize. In 1545, Spanish colonists began mining a huge silver mountain at Potosi, in today's Bolivia. Brazil grew rich from sugar and, later, gold. Catholic missionaries also came to spread their faith. Some protected Indigenous people from abuse, while mission life also pressed Indigenous people to give up their own beliefs.

words.d: a land ruled by a distant country
large regions of Spanish America, each ruled by a viceroy in the king's name
people sent to spread a religion to others

look.title: A Line on a Map
look.text: Picture two kings in Europe drawing a line down a map of lands they have barely seen. One side goes to Spain and the other to Portugal. Millions of people live in those lands, speaking hundreds of languages. None of them has signed the treaty.
look.prompt: What does this scene show about how colonial rulers thought about the peoples already living in the Americas?

check.q: What was a viceroyalty?
choices: A farm owned by an Indigenous family
A large region ruled by a viceroy in the king's name
A treaty between two European kings
check.why: Spain governed its American lands through viceroyalties, each led by a viceroy.

check.q: Which land did Portugal receive after the Treaty of Tordesillas?
choices: The eastern part, which became Brazil
check.why: The reading says Portugal received the eastern part, which became Brazil, and Spain claimed most of the rest.

check.q: What was the main purpose of colonies for the ruling country?
choices: To make money, for example from silver and sugar
To build roads for private travelers
check.why: Colonies were meant to make money. Potosi silver and Brazilian sugar are examples.

lessons.title: The Encomienda
lessons.mainIdea: The encomienda gave Spanish colonists the right to Indigenous people's labor and tribute, and it led to terrible abuse.
reading: After the conquest, the Spanish crown rewarded many conquerors with an *encomienda*. This was a grant of the labor and tribute of the Indigenous people in a certain area. In return, the holder, called an encomendero, was supposed to protect them and teach them Christianity. In law, the Indigenous people were not his property. In practice, many encomenderos worked people very hard and punished them cruelly.

At the same time, diseases from Europe, such as smallpox and measles, spread through the Americas. Indigenous peoples had no earlier contact with these illnesses. Terrible *epidemics* killed a very large share of the population in the 1500s. Scholars debate the exact numbers, but in many regions most people died within a few generations. War, forced labor and hunger made the losses worse.

Other forms of forced labor followed. In Peru, Spanish officials took over the old Inca mit'a. They used it to send Indigenous men in turns to work in the silver mines of Potosi, where many died. Indigenous communities pushed back. They filed lawsuits in Spanish courts, fled, and sometimes rose up. In 1780, Tupac Amaru II led a large revolt in Peru against colonial abuses.

words.d: a Spanish grant of the labor and tribute of Indigenous people in an area
outbreaks of disease that spread to many people at once
work people must do against their will

look.title: The Law and the Field
look.text: On paper, the law says: the encomendero must protect the people and may not own them. In the field, a village elder tells a priest that the men are gone for weeks at a time and the children have too little to eat. The encomendero lives far away and rarely visits.
look.prompt: Why can a law say one thing while life on the ground is very different? Who could enforce the law?

check.q: What did an encomienda give a Spanish colonist?
choices: Ownership of a silver mine in Spain
The labor and tribute of Indigenous people in an area
A seat on the king's council
check.why: An encomienda was a grant of Indigenous people's labor and tribute. The holder was supposed to protect them.

check.q: Why did European diseases kill so many Indigenous people?
choices: They had no doctors of their own
They had no earlier contact with those illnesses
They refused all food from Europe
check.why: The reading says Indigenous peoples had no earlier contact with diseases like smallpox, so epidemics spread widely.

check.q: How did Spanish officials use the old Inca mit'a?
choices: To build new roads for chasqui runners
To fill storehouses for hungry families
To pay Indigenous workers high wages
To send Indigenous men in turns to the silver mines of Potosi
check.why: Spanish officials took over mit'a and used it to send men in turns to the Potosi mines.

lessons.title: Voices Against Abuse
lessons.mainIdea: Some Spaniards, like Bartolome de las Casas, argued against the abuse of Indigenous people, and the crown passed laws to limit it.
reading: Bartolome de las Casas came to the Caribbean as a young colonist and held Indigenous laborers himself. Around 1514 he changed his mind. He gave up his laborers, became a Dominican friar, and spent about fifty years speaking against the cruelty he had seen. He argued that Indigenous people were fully human, with rights to their lands and freedom.

Las Casas argued with other scholars in Spain. In a famous debate at Valladolid in 1550 and 1551, he faced Juan Gines de Sepulveda. Sepulveda claimed that conquest was just. Las Casas said it was not. His voice helped push the king to pass the *New Laws* of 1542. These laws aimed to end new encomiendas and to stop the enslavement of Indigenous people.

The New Laws had limited effect. Colonists protested so strongly that parts were soon softened. Las Casas also has a mixed record. Early on, he suggested bringing enslaved Africans to spare Indigenous workers. He later wrote that he deeply regretted this. His life shows how a *reformer* can change his views and still leave a complicated legacy.

words.d: Spanish laws of 1542 meant to limit the encomienda and ban enslaving Indigenous people
a person who works to change a system to make it fairer
a member of a Catholic religious order who lives by vows and often preaches

look.title: A Friar's Warning
look.text: Las Casas described Indigenous people as gentle and patient, and he accused the Spanish of treating them with a cruelty greater than wild animals. He wrote to warn the future king about what was happening in the Indies.
look.cite: Bartolome de las Casas, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, 1552 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Las Casas wanted to shock the king into action. How might that goal affect how he wrote? What makes his account still important?

check.q: What were the New Laws of 1542?
choices: Spanish laws meant to limit the encomienda and ban enslaving Indigenous people
Laws that created the casta paintings
Laws that ended slavery in all colonies
check.why: The New Laws aimed to end new encomiendas and stop the enslavement of Indigenous people.

check.q: What did Las Casas argue in the debate at Valladolid?
choices: That the conquest was not just and Indigenous people had rights
That colonists should get more encomiendas
That Spain should give Brazil to Portugal
check.why: Las Casas argued against Sepulveda, who claimed conquest was just.

check.q: Why does the reading call Las Casas's legacy complicated?
choices: He first suggested bringing enslaved Africans, which he later regretted
He wrote the casta paintings' labels
check.why: The reading says Las Casas early on suggested bringing enslaved Africans and later deeply regretted it.

lessons.title: Peninsulares and Criollos
lessons.mainIdea: In Spanish America, people born in Spain held top posts, and American-born Spaniards resented being ranked below them.
reading: In a Spanish colonial city, two men of Spanish families might live on the same street. One was born in Spain. He was a *peninsular*, from the Iberian Peninsula. The other was born in Mexico City. He was a *criollo*, or creole. Both claimed Spanish ancestry. But the crown often gave the highest posts, such as viceroy, bishop and top judge, to peninsulares.

Criollos were often rich. They owned land, mines and businesses, and many were well educated. Still, they felt shut out of the highest offices, especially in the late 1700s, when Spain sent more officials from Spain. Over time, many criollos began to think of themselves as Americans more than Spaniards. Their frustration later helped fuel movements for independence in the early 1800s.

This ranking is part of a larger *social hierarchy*. Birthplace, ancestry, wealth, religion and job all shaped a person's place. The crown and church kept careful records of births and marriages that often listed a person's group. Portuguese Brazil had its own ranks, with people born in Portugal at the top and enslaved Africans at the bottom.

words.d: a person in Spanish America who was born in Spain
a person of Spanish ancestry born in the Americas; also called a creole
a ranking of groups in a society by status and power

look.title: Two Cousins
look.text: Two cousins share a grandfather in Spain. One is born in Seville and sails to Mexico as a young man. The other is born in Mexico City. Both study law. When a high judge's post opens, the cousin born in Seville gets it.
look.prompt: Which cousin is the peninsular and which is the criollo? How might the criollo cousin feel, and why?

check.q: What was a criollo?
choices: A person born in Spain living in the Americas
A person of Spanish and Indigenous ancestry
An enslaved worker in a silver mine
A person of Spanish ancestry born in the Americas
check.why: Criollos were of Spanish ancestry but born in the Americas. Peninsulares were born in Spain.

check.q: Why did many criollos feel frustrated?
choices: The top posts often went to people born in Spain
They were not allowed to own land
They were forced to work in mines
They had no access to education
check.why: The reading says criollos were often rich and educated but felt shut out of the highest offices.

check.q: Which things shaped a person's place in the colonial hierarchy?
choices: Birthplace, ancestry, wealth, religion and job
Only which city a person lived in
check.why: The reading lists birthplace, ancestry, wealth, religion and job as shaping a person's place.

lessons.title: Mixed Societies
lessons.mainIdea: Colonial Latin America grew into mixed societies of Spanish, Indigenous and African people, and the law ranked these groups.
reading: Spanish America was never only Spanish. Indigenous people were the largest group in many regions for centuries. Africans, most brought by force, formed large communities, especially near the coasts. Over generations, many families mixed. A *mestizo* was a person of Spanish and Indigenous ancestry. A mulato was a person of Spanish and African ancestry. Many other combinations had names.

The Spanish used the word *castas* for people of mixed ancestry. Colonial law and custom ranked these groups. People of mixed ancestry often paid different taxes, could be barred from some schools, guilds and church posts, and faced limits on carrying weapons. Indigenous people lived under their own set of laws, with their own towns and leaders, and paid tribute to the crown.

The labels were not as fixed as the laws suggest. A person could be written down as one group in a baptism record and another in a marriage record. Wealth, clothing, language and friends could change how others saw someone. In the late 1700s, some people even paid the crown for official papers that raised their status. Historians see these changes as signs that the system was often bent by the people inside it.

words.d: a person of mixed Spanish and Indigenous ancestry
the colonial Spanish name for people of mixed ancestry and the ranks given to them
the people a person is descended from

look.title: One Person, Two Records
look.text: A church record from 1745 lists a baby girl as mestiza. In 1765, her marriage record lists her as espanola, or Spanish. She has not changed. But her family has become richer, and the priest who wrote the second record knew them well.
look.prompt: What does this example tell you about how fixed the casta labels really were?

check.q: What was a mestizo?
choices: A person of Spanish and African ancestry
A person of Spanish and Indigenous ancestry
check.why: The reading defines a mestizo as a person of Spanish and Indigenous ancestry. Mulato meant Spanish and African ancestry.

check.q: How could the casta system limit people of mixed ancestry?
choices: It required them to live in Spain
It forced them to become viceroys
It gave them the highest government offices
It could bar them from some schools, guilds and church posts
check.why: The reading says people of mixed ancestry could be barred from some schools, guilds and church posts.

check.q: What evidence shows casta labels could change?
choices: The same person could be listed as different groups in different records
Every person kept one label from birth to death
Only the king could write a label
check.why: The reading says a person could appear as one group in a baptism record and another in a marriage record.

lessons.title: The Casta Paintings
lessons.mainIdea: Casta paintings of the 1700s showed an idealized ranking of mixed families, and historians read them as ideas, not snapshots.
reading: In the 1700s, painters in New Spain made sets of *casta paintings*. A set was often sixteen panels. Each panel showed a mother, a father and a child, with a label naming each person's group. The painter Miguel Cabrera painted a famous set in 1763. Many sets were sent to Spain, where people were curious about life in the Americas.

The paintings follow a pattern. Families at the start of a set, with Spanish ancestry, often wear fine clothes in pleasant homes. Families later in the set, farther from Spanish ancestry, often look poorer. Some panels show quarrels. The paintings also show food, fruit, clothing and trades of the colony in rich detail, so they are useful for other kinds of history too.

Historians treat casta paintings as *primary sources* that show an idea, not a photograph of real life. They show how colonial elites wanted to explain and rank a mixed society. Some scholars also see pride in them, a way for criollo painters to show the richness of their homeland. Reading them well means asking who made them, who paid for them, and whom they left out.

words.d: sets of 1700s paintings from New Spain showing families labeled by mixed ancestry
documents or objects made at the time being studied
the small group with the most wealth, power or status in a society

look.title: Reading a Panel
look.text: In one panel, a Spanish father in a lace collar stands beside an Indigenous mother in a woven huipil blouse. Their son holds a basket of fruit. The room has a carved chest and a painted screen. A label at the bottom names the three groups.
look.prompt: What does this panel want a viewer in Spain to believe? What real details of colonial life can you still learn from it?

check.q: What did a typical casta painting show?
choices: A map of the Treaty of Tordesillas
A mother, father and child with labels naming their groups
A battle between Spain and the Inca
A portrait of the king of Spain
check.why: Each panel showed a family with a label naming each person's group.

check.q: How do historians read casta paintings?
choices: As exact portraits of real families
As laws passed by the viceroy
As sources that show an idea about ranking, not a photograph of real life
check.why: The reading says historians treat casta paintings as primary sources showing an idea held by elites.

check.q: Which painter made a famous casta set in 1763?
check.why: The reading names Miguel Cabrera. Las Casas was a friar and Guaman Poma an Andean writer.

lessons.title: Twelve Million People
lessons.mainIdea: From the 1500s to the 1800s, about 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships bound for the Americas.
reading: The *transatlantic slave trade* carried captive Africans across the Atlantic Ocean to the Americas. It lasted from the early 1500s to the 1860s. The SlaveVoyages database, built by historians from ship records, estimates that about 12.5 million people were forced onto ships. About 10.7 million survived the voyage. Most came from West and West-Central Africa.

Traders from Portugal, Britain, France, the Netherlands, Spain, Denmark and the Americas all took part. On the African coast they bought captives, often taken in wars or raids, from African traders and rulers in exchange for cloth, guns, metal goods and other items. Some African states grew rich from the trade. Others were torn apart by it. Many Africans resisted capture and fought back.

The voyage was called the *Middle Passage*. People were chained below deck in crowded, airless spaces for weeks or months. Disease, hunger and brutality killed well over a million people at sea. Captives sometimes rose up on ships or refused to eat. Those who arrived were sold in ports across the Americas. Most were sent to work on plantations.

words.d: the forced shipping of captive Africans across the Atlantic to the Americas
the voyage across the Atlantic on which captive Africans were carried
large farms that grew one cash crop, often worked by enslaved people

look.title: Where Captives Arrived
look.cite: SlaveVoyages, Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, estimates of arrivals, 1501-1866
look.prompt: Which region received the most captives? About how many times more went to Brazil than to mainland North America?

check.q: About how many Africans were forced onto ships in the transatlantic slave trade?
check.why: The SlaveVoyages database estimates about 12.5 million people were forced onto ships, and about 10.7 million survived.

check.q: What was the Middle Passage?
choices: The voyage across the Atlantic for captive Africans
A trade route from Spain to Asia
check.why: The Middle Passage was the crossing on which captives were chained below deck for weeks or months.

check.q: According to the data, which region received the most captives?
check.why: The SlaveVoyages estimates show about 4.8 million arrivals in Brazil, far more than any other region.

lessons.title: Slavery in Brazil and the Caribbean
lessons.mainIdea: Sugar plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean depended on enslaved Africans, and the work was so deadly that owners kept buying more captives.
reading: On a Caribbean island in the 1700s, a *sugar mill* runs day and night at harvest time. Enslaved workers cut cane in the hot fields, then feed it into rollers and boil the juice in huge kettles. Burns and crushed limbs are common. Sugar was the main crop that drew enslaved Africans to Brazil and to islands like Jamaica, Barbados and Saint-Domingue.

The work was so harsh that many enslaved people died young. In many sugar colonies, deaths outnumbered births. Planters found it cheaper to buy new captives than to improve conditions. This is why far more Africans were shipped to Brazil and the Caribbean than to North America. In Saint-Domingue, by the late 1700s, enslaved people made up about nine out of ten people in the colony.

Enslaved people built lives and cultures under this pressure. They kept African languages, music, foods and faiths, and blended them with new ones. Religions such as Candomble in Brazil and Vodou in Haiti grew from African traditions mixed with Catholic practices. In Brazil, enslaved people could sometimes buy their freedom, so a large free Black population grew there. Freedom, though, did not mean equality.

words.d: a place where sugarcane is crushed and its juice is boiled into sugar
a crop grown to sell, not for the farmer's family to eat
a Brazilian religion that grew from West African traditions

look.title: A Survivor's Account
look.text: Olaudah Equiano, who wrote that he was taken from West Africa as a child, described the hold of the slave ship. He told of the crowding, the heat and the smell, the cries of the sick, and his wish to die rather than go on.
look.cite: Olaudah Equiano, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, 1789 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Equiano published his book in London while people were arguing about ending the slave trade. How might his account have affected readers?

check.q: What was a cash crop?
choices: A crop grown only for the family to eat
A crop used to pay the Inca
check.why: A cash crop is grown to sell. Sugar was the main cash crop in Brazil and the Caribbean.

check.q: Why were so many captives shipped to sugar colonies?
choices: Harsh work killed so many people that planters kept buying more
Sugar plantations needed very few workers
Enslaved people there lived longer than anywhere else
Laws there banned buying new captives
check.why: The reading says deaths outnumbered births in many sugar colonies, so planters kept buying new captives.

check.q: Which religion grew from African traditions in Brazil?
check.why: Candomble in Brazil grew from West African traditions mixed with Catholic practices.

lessons.title: Slavery in the United States
lessons.mainIdea: Fewer captives came to North America, but slavery there grew through births to about four million people by 1860.
reading: About 400,000 captive Africans were brought to mainland North America, a small share of the whole trade. Yet by 1860 there were nearly four million enslaved people in the United States. The difference came from natural increase: births outnumbered deaths there. Slavery in the United States was *hereditary*. A child born to an enslaved mother was enslaved for life.

Enslaved people grew tobacco, rice and, above all, cotton. After Eli Whitney's cotton gin of 1793 made cleaning cotton faster, cotton spread across the Deep South. Enslaved families were often split apart by sale. Laws in many Southern states made it a crime to teach enslaved people to read. The United States banned bringing in new captives from abroad in 1808, but the trade within the country kept growing.

Enslaved people resisted in many ways. Some worked slowly, broke tools or ran away. Some, like Harriet Tubman, escaped and returned to lead others to freedom. Others kept faith, family and songs alive in secret. People who opposed slavery were called *abolitionists*. Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in 1838 and became one of the most famous abolitionist speakers and writers.

words.d: passed down from parent to child
people who worked to end slavery
population growth that happens when births outnumber deaths

look.title: Enslaved People in the United States
look.cite: U.S. Census Bureau, decennial censuses of 1790, 1820, 1840 and 1860 (rounded)
look.prompt: About how much did the enslaved population grow from 1790 to 1860? What does the chapter say caused that growth?

check.q: What does hereditary slavery mean?
choices: Only prisoners of war were enslaved
A child born to an enslaved mother was enslaved for life
People could choose to become enslaved
check.why: Hereditary means passed from parent to child. In the United States, children of enslaved mothers were enslaved.

check.q: Why did the enslaved population in the United States grow so large?
choices: Most captives in the whole trade went to North America
The trade from Africa grew after 1808
Births outnumbered deaths, so it grew by natural increase
check.why: Only about 400,000 captives came, but natural increase raised the number to nearly four million by 1860.

check.q: Who escaped slavery in 1838 and became a famous abolitionist speaker?
check.why: Frederick Douglass escaped in 1838 and became a leading abolitionist speaker and writer.

lessons.title: Maroons and Everyday Resistance
lessons.mainIdea: Enslaved people resisted in every colony, from quiet daily acts to whole free communities of runaways called maroons.
reading: Deep in the hills of northeast Brazil in the 1600s stood Palmares. It was a *quilombo*, a settlement of people who had escaped slavery. Palmares grew to thousands of people and lasted for most of the century. Its people farmed, traded and defended their towns against many attacks. Portuguese forces destroyed it in 1694. Its last leader, Zumbi, was killed in 1695. Brazil honors him today with a Black Consciousness Day on November 20.

Communities of escaped people were called *maroons* in English. They formed in Jamaica, Suriname, Colombia, Florida and many other places. In Jamaica, maroon fighters forced the British to sign treaties in 1739 recognizing their towns. In Colombia, San Basilio de Palenque was founded by people who escaped slavery and still exists today.

Most resistance was quieter. Enslaved people slowed work, broke tools, pretended to be ill, or ran away for short times. They kept their names, languages and faiths. Parents taught children their family history. Historians call these everyday acts *resistance* because they pushed back against a system that tried to control every part of life.

words.d: a Brazilian settlement of people who escaped slavery
people who escaped slavery and formed free communities
actions taken to push back against control or injustice

lessons.title: The Haitian Revolution
lessons.mainIdea: From 1791 to 1804, enslaved people in Saint-Domingue overthrew slavery and French rule and founded Haiti.
reading: Saint-Domingue, the French colony on the western part of the island of Hispaniola, was the richest colony in the Caribbean. It produced huge amounts of sugar and coffee. About half a million enslaved people worked there. In August 1791 they rose up in a massive revolt in the northern plain. It became the *Haitian Revolution*, the only revolt of enslaved people in history that created a new nation.

The war was long and complex. Spain and Britain sent troops. In 1793 and 1794, French officials and then the French government in Paris ended slavery in the colony. *Toussaint Louverture*, a formerly enslaved man, became the leading general and governor. When Napoleon sent a large army in 1802 to restore French control, Toussaint was captured and shipped to France, where he died in prison in 1803.

Jean-Jacques Dessalines led the final fight. Yellow fever and fierce resistance destroyed much of the French army. On January 1, 1804, Dessalines declared the independence of Haiti, the second independent nation in the Americas after the United States. The war was brutal on all sides. Afterward, many nations refused to recognize Haiti, and in 1825 France forced it to pay a huge *indemnity* in return for recognition.

words.d: the 1791 to 1804 uprising that ended slavery and French rule in Saint-Domingue
a formerly enslaved general who led the Haitian Revolution until his capture in 1802
a payment demanded to make up for a loss

lessons.title: Abolition and Its Legacies
lessons.mainIdea: Slavery was abolished across the Americas between the 1790s and 1888, but its effects on inequality lasted long after.
reading: *Abolition* means ending slavery by law. It came country by country. Mexico abolished slavery in 1829. Britain ended it in most of its colonies in 1834. In the United States, the Civil War led to the Thirteenth Amendment, adopted in 1865. Illinois was the first state to ratify it, on February 1, 1865. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to end slavery, with the Golden Law of May 13, 1888.

Abolition came from many forces. Enslaved people resisted and escaped. Abolitionists, Black and white, wrote, spoke and organized. Religious groups, such as Quakers, called slavery a sin. Some economists argued that free labor worked better. Wars and revolutions also broke slavery apart. Historians still debate how much each of these causes mattered in each place.

Freedom did not bring equality. Formerly enslaved people often got no land and faced unfair laws, low pay and violence. Across Latin America, the old ranking by ancestry left lasting gaps in wealth and schooling. Scholars and citizens today debate how large these *legacies* are and what, if anything, should be done. They agree that the history helps explain patterns of inequality that can still be seen.

words.d: ending slavery by law
effects of the past that continue into later times
the 1865 change to the U.S. Constitution that abolished slavery
